questions.q: As defined on this page, pharmacokinetics is the study of:
opts: Movement of drugs in the body after intake through any route
Binding of drugs to their specific receptors
Variation of drug response between individuals
questions.exp: Pharmacokinetics = study of movement of drugs in the body after intake through any route; the drug-induced change in the body is pharmacodynamics. (Book p1)

questions.q: Pharmacodynamics is defined as:
opts: The movement of the drug within the body after intake
The chemical breakdown of the drug in the liver
The elimination of the drug via the kidney
The drug-induced change in the body
questions.exp: Pharmacodynamics = drug-induced change in the body (what the drug does to the body). (Book p1)

questions.q: In the course-of-drug flowchart, which processes are colour-coded as pharmacokinetics?
opts: Drug, binds to target and effect
Intake, binding and onset of action
Adipose storage, redistribution and tubular secretion
questions.exp: The legend marks absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion as pharmacokinetics; the drug, binding to target and effect are marked as pharmacodynamics. (Book p1)

questions.q: According to the flowchart legend, which trio is treated as pharmacodynamic events?
questions.exp: The legend highlights the drug itself, 'binds to target' and 'effect' as pharmacodynamics. (Book p1)

questions.q: A drug is taken orally. Per the flowchart, the first pharmacokinetic step it undergoes is:
questions.exp: The orally taken drug undergoes absorption first, and only then reaches the systemic circulation. (Book p1)

questions.q: Immediately after absorption, the drug enters the:
questions.exp: Absorption delivers the drug into the systemic circulation; from there it can be distributed (e.g., to adipose tissue) or carried on to the remaining drug steps. (Book p1)

questions.q: In the flowchart, the movement of drug toward the adipose tissue is labelled:
questions.exp: The arrow carrying drug to the adipose tissue is labelled distribution. (Book p1)

questions.q: Some drugs reach the adipose tissue by a variant of distribution termed:
questions.exp: The second arrow to adipose tissue reads 'Some drugs: Redistribution' — these drugs shift into fat after entering the circulation. (Book p1)

questions.q: Which set correctly lists the features of drugs reaching adipose tissue?
opts: Very short acting, high lipid solubility, crosses the BBB
Long acting, water soluble, confined to plasma
Very short acting, water soluble, cannot cross the BBB
Long acting, high lipid solubility, excluded from the CNS
questions.exp: Drugs reaching adipose tissue are very short acting, have increased lipid solubility and cross the blood–brain barrier — e.g., the anaesthetics propofol and thiopentone. (Book p1)

questions.q: Drugs that partition into adipose tissue share which solubility profile?
questions.exp: Adipose-seeking drugs have increased lipid solubility, which also lets them cross the BBB. (Book p1)

questions.q: Owing to their high lipid solubility, the adipose-reaching anaesthetics readily cross the:
questions.exp: Increased lipid solubility → crosses the blood–brain barrier, the property exploited by intravenous anaesthetics like propofol and thiopentone. (Book p1)

questions.q: The intravenous anaesthetics cited as examples of drugs reaching adipose tissue are:
questions.exp: The examples given are the anaesthetics propofol and thiopentone. (Book p1)

questions.q: A patient wakes within minutes of stopping a propofol infusion. Per the flowchart, propofol's 'very short acting' behaviour is best explained by its:
questions.exp: Lipid-soluble anaesthetics such as propofol and thiopentone move into adipose tissue (distribution/redistribution) and are therefore very short acting. (Book p1)

questions.q: In the flowchart, the systemic circulation containing the remaining drug passes it next to which event?
questions.exp: Systemic circulation containing the remaining drug → binds to target. (Book p1)

questions.q: The drug produces its clinical effect only after it:
questions.exp: 'Binds to target' → 'effect': binding to the target is the pharmacodynamic step that produces the effect. (Book p1)

questions.q: How do most drugs bind to their target?
questions.exp: Most drugs bind reversibly; hence breakdown of the bond later releases the drug back into the circulation. (Book p1)

questions.q: According to the loop in the flowchart, breakdown of the drug–target bond causes the drug to:
questions.exp: Because most drugs bind reversibly, breakdown of the bond returns the drug to the systemic circulation. (Book p1)

questions.q: Metabolism in the liver breaks the drug down and makes it more:
questions.exp: Liver metabolism = breakdown that makes the drug water soluble, preparing it for excretion. (Book p1)

questions.q: The purpose of converting the drug into a water-soluble form is to promote its:
questions.exp: Once made water soluble, most drugs pass via the systemic circulation to the kidney for excretion (some via the gut). (Book p1)

questions.q: Per the flowchart, most drugs are excreted through the:
questions.exp: Most drugs are excreted via the systemic circulation into the kidney; the gut handles the remainder. (Book p1)

questions.q: Besides the kidney, the other excretory route shown is the:
questions.exp: Excretion = most drugs via systemic circulation → kidney, and some via the gut. (Book p1)

questions.sec: Course of drug through the body
questions.q: Arrange the course of an orally administered drug in the correct order:
opts: Absorption → systemic circulation → target binding → effect → hepatic metabolism → excretion
Absorption → hepatic metabolism → target binding → systemic circulation → effect
Systemic circulation → absorption → excretion → target binding → effect
Target binding → absorption → distribution → excretion → effect
questions.exp: Oral drug → absorption → systemic circulation → binds to target → effect; remaining drug is metabolised in the liver to a water-soluble form and excreted via the kidney (most drugs) or the gut. (Book p1)

units.title: PK vs PD: The Two Definitions
units.sec: INTRODUCTION TO PHARMACOKINETICS AND PHARMACODYNAMICS · p1
units.guide: Pharmacokinetics is the study of a drug's movement through the body after intake by any route; pharmacodynamics is the change the drug induces in the body. The figure flags absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion as the kinetic processes, and the drug, its binding to the target and the resulting effect as the dynamic events.

units.title: Absorption → Distribution → Adipose
units.sec: Course of drug through the body · p1
units.guide: An oral drug is absorbed into the systemic circulation and may be distributed to adipose tissue — some drugs by redistribution. Adipose-seeking drugs are very short acting, highly lipid soluble and cross the BBB, like the anaesthetics propofol and thiopentone.

units.title: Binding, Metabolism & Excretion
units.sec: Course of drug through the body · p1
units.guide: The circulating drug binds its target — most drugs bind reversibly — and the effect follows; breakdown of the bond frees the drug back into the circulation. The liver then breaks the remaining drug down to a water-soluble form, which is excreted mostly via the kidney and partly via the gut.
